agent_notes: The verb has no stated object, and the five English versions split: KJV/ASV/Webster supply 'the LORD' as object of 'I love'; YLT leaves 'I have loved' bare, as the Hebrew does. I keep the Hebrew's bare 'I love' in the literal layer, with [him] in brackets. Meiri and Metzudat David read the verse as inverted ('I love the LORD because...'), Rashi reads 'I long that the LORD hear', and Ibn Ezra reads 'how I loved that he hear'. The first is the plain reading and the one I follow.

Tense: 'yishma' is imperfect while the parallel 'hitah' (v.2) is perfect. I rendered it as a present habitual ('hears') in the dramatic layer, and 'will hear / hears' in the literal layer. Meiri takes the imperfect as standing for the past; I did not follow him, since the habitual sense fits 'in my days I call' in v.2.
STEPBible glosses 'yishma' as 'he has heard' (perfect). The form is imperfect (HVqi3ms), so I glossed it 'he hears'.

The most disputed verse of the window. 'he'emanti ki adaber' (HVhp1cs + ki + imperfect) can mean 'I believed even when I spoke', 'I believed, therefore I speak' (KJV, Paul at 2 Cor 4:13 quoting the Septuagint, where the psalm is numbered 115), or 'I believe when I speak'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra tie it to specific stories (Ziba and Mephibosheth, 2 Sam 16:4; a retort) that I could not check beyond what the packet cites. I translate 'I believed, [even] when I would speak' in the literal layer, which keeps 'ki' open, and say so in the commentary.
STEPBible glosses 'aniti' as 'I am afflicted'. The form is perfect (HVqp1cs) so 'I was afflicted' is the better rendering.

agent_notes: 'bechafzi' (in my haste) is rendered 'in my alarm' in the dramatic layer, keeping the sense of hurried flight. BBE has 'fear', which is an interpretation: the Hebrew root chafaz means to hurry, to be alarmed. Rashi's link to 1 Sam 23:26 (David hurrying to get away from Saul) is cited as his, and I do not adopt it.

agent_notes: 'tagmulohi' is an Aramaic-looking form with the ending -ohi for -av ('his'), which Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion all explain by Aramaic 'alohi' = 'alav'. The word occurs once in the Bible (hapax legomenon, H8408), so the gloss is by derivation from gamal. I could not verify the HALOT entry, so the claim in the note rests on the commentaries.

history.note: [consider] Drop Ibn Ezra from the list of those who hold the Aramaic reading, or say that he mentions it and prefers two words. (Ibn Ezra on PS.116.12: "ולפי דעתי: שהיא שתי מלות")

agent_notes: 'Cup of salvation(s)': the noun is plural (yeshuot), an intensive or abstract plural; I kept 'salvations' in the literal layer. Whether the cup is a libation/thanksgiving drink or a 'portion' as in Ps 16:5 is disputed (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri); the dramatic layer follows the ritual reading but the commentary flags the other.

The five English versions all say 'precious' and 'death of his saints'. I kept 'costly' and 'weighty' because Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion all read יָקָר as 'heavy, hard' (cf. Ps 49:9), so the verse says that death reaching the faithful is a grave matter in the LORD's eyes. The dramatic layer follows the reviewer's request and has no comparison.

STEPBible glosses הַמָּוְתָה as 'the death <towards>' (a directional ה). I glossed it as 'the death', with the ending in a note. Ibn Ezra denies that the ה marks a feminine and compares it to שְׁאוֹלָה, and Rashi compares הַבַּיְתָה, so the sense of motion ('death coming to') is a reading, not a certainty.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses anah as 'I beg you'; I kept 'ah, now' / 'I beg' as the interjection of entreaty, which the commentators (Ibn Ezra, Metzudat Zion) read as thanks or plea. YLT's 'cause it to come' reads a different word and I did not follow it.

agent_notes: The consonants of 'metzarei' (H4712 'distresses') are close to 'metzarim', 'straits', as in Ps 118:5. I render 'straits' in the literal layer to keep the narrowness (root צר) that is repeated in 'tzarah' ('trouble') in the same verse. Rashi glosses 'borders of Sheol'; I list this as an alternative in the commentary.

STEPBible glosses 'ekra' as past ('I called'). The form is imperfect (HVqi1cs), and the verse follows v.2 'in my days I will call', so I translate it as a present habitual in the literal layer. The dramatic layer narrates it as a past ('I called') because the speech that follows reads as a remembered cry; this is a choice, and KJV's 'then' is not in the Hebrew.

history.note: [consider] Paraphrase Radak as one of three spellings with he, stressed on the first syllable. (Radak on PS.116.4: "וזה מן השלשה הכתובים בה"א, וקריאת האל"ף מלעיל, כי האל"ף קמוצה והנו"ן דגושה")

agent_notes: 'daloti' is a perfect ('I was low'), as Radak and Meiri note from its final stress. 'yehoshia' is a jussive-looking imperfect form that KJV/ASV/Webster read as past ('he helped/saved me'); Radak and Meiri read it as 'he will save me'. I follow STEPBible's 'he saved' in the glosses and the translations, as the sequel (v.8, 'you have rescued') confirms the past sense.

The spellings 'limnuchayekhi' and 'alayekhi' keep an old long form of the 2fs suffix (-ekhi), which Metzudat Zion calls an extra yod. I glossed the suffix as 'your'. Targum has 'return, my soul, to the house of your rest' (bet menuchayekh), which is its own addition.

history.note: [consider] Say 'on the noun and the preposition'. (PS.116.7: "לִמְנוּחָיְכִי … עָלָיְכִי")

agent_notes: The Hebrew shifts to second person ('you rescued') within a psalm that has so far spoken about the LORD in the third. I keep the shift visible in the literal layer and in the dramatic layer, and I explain it in the commentary as the moment the self-address of v.7 turns to address God.

'artzot haChayyim' is a plural construct ('lands of the living'). KJV/ASV/Webster/BBE all make it singular. The plural is a real feature of the Hebrew; Radak reads 'the cities of Israel', Meiri 'the world to come' or the Land of Israel. I do not choose between them.
